chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
title: Stable bands: Don Redman, Fletcher Henderson, Chick Webb broadcasts
summary: McRae says the great bands stayed together like families, and listeners across the country ran to the radio for Henderson and Webb.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: And it was very little bands back there. It was so well put together with personalities, you know, that it wasn't much changing in the band.
Like, you take the Don Redman Band -- that was a good band, you know.
And there was the personality in the band put together so, just like a big family. Wasn't no arguments. It was just like a classic thing.

These guys would come out, you know, play together. You had a lot of bands, you know -- Take Fletcher Henderson. That was another classic band. We called him the daddy of the big band. The man who really brought big bands out (inaudible) any of the white bands.
He was the daddy of the big bands. Big sound, Fletcher Henderson. Everybody looked up to Fletcher Henderson.
If you wouldn't be home, you'd run to get home if Fletcher Henderson is going to be on the air at five o'clock. You'd run to get home to your radio.

know, "eight o'clock, six o'clock." Same way when Chick Webb used to broadcast.

When we travelled throughout the west, people will say, "Hey, we used to catch yall in Kansas City," these guys told us. "We catch you on the air every afternoon at six o'clock playing from the Savoy Ballroom, man. Listening to you -- man, we hear you playing."
"See you made a break, wonder how you are going to get out of it," you know. People be listening to you all over the country.
